question_bank.title: Forces and Motion: Basics — Physics Assessment

questions.question_text: When the forces acting on an object are balanced, the object will:
options: Remain at rest or move at constant velocity
questions.correct_answer: Remain at rest or move at constant velocity
questions.explanation: Balanced forces produce zero net force, so there is no acceleration (Newton's First Law).

questions.question_text: Unbalanced forces acting on an object cause:
questions.explanation: A non-zero net force changes the object's velocity (Newton's Second Law).

questions.question_text: The SI unit of force is the:
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N) in the SI system.

questions.question_text: If the net force on a 4 kg object is 8 N, its acceleration is:
questions.explanation: From F = ma, a = F/m = 8/4 = 2 m/s².

questions.question_text: Friction always acts in the direction opposite to the motion of an object.
questions.explanation: Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact.

questions.question_text: Newton's First Law states that an object in motion stays in motion unless acted on by an unbalanced force.
questions.explanation: This is the law of inertia.

questions.question_text: In the tug-of-war screen, adding more people on one side increases the:
questions.explanation: More applied force on one side creates a larger net force arrow.

questions.question_text: For the same mass, a larger net force produces:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is directly proportional to net force when mass is constant (F = ma).

questions.question_text: State Newton's Second Law as an equation.
questions.explanation: Force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.

questions.question_text: Name one variable you can change in the simulation to observe its effect on acceleration.
questions.explanation: You can change applied force, mass, or friction and observe the effect on motion.

questions.question_text: On a position–time graph, the gradient (slope) represents:
questions.explanation: The slope of a position–time graph gives velocity.

questions.question_text: On a velocity–time graph, the gradient represents:
questions.explanation: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.

questions.question_text: Uniform motion is shown on a velocity–time graph as:
questions.explanation: Constant velocity appears as a horizontal line on a v–t graph.

questions.question_text: Motion with constant positive acceleration produces a position–time graph that is:
questions.explanation: Constant acceleration gives a curved (parabolic) position–time graph.

questions.question_text: A negative velocity means the object is moving in the opposite direction to the positive axis.
questions.explanation: Sign of velocity indicates direction of motion along the axis.

questions.question_text: When acceleration is zero, velocity remains constant.
questions.explanation: Zero acceleration means no change in velocity.

questions.question_text: If the velocity–time graph is a horizontal line at 2 m/s, the motion is:
questions.explanation: Constant velocity of 2 m/s means uniform motion.

questions.question_text: If the slope of the velocity–time graph is zero, the acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Zero slope on v–t means acceleration is zero.

questions.question_text: What physical quantity is represented by the area under a velocity–time graph?
questions.explanation: Area under a v–t graph gives displacement.

questions.question_text: Name one kinematic quantity you can read from the simulation graphs.
questions.explanation: The sim displays position, velocity, and acceleration graphs.

question_bank.title: Energy Skate Park: Basics — Physics Assessment

questions.question_text: At the highest point of the track (without friction), most of the skater's energy is:
questions.explanation: At maximum height, speed is lowest and gravitational PE is greatest.

questions.question_text: When friction is turned on in the simulation, mechanical energy is converted mainly into:
questions.explanation: Friction converts mechanical energy to heat (thermal energy).

questions.question_text: Without friction, the total mechanical energy of the skater as they move along the track:
questions.explanation: Mechanical energy is conserved when friction is negligible.

questions.question_text: As the skater moves down a ramp, kinetic energy generally increases.
questions.explanation: PE converts to KE as height decreases.

questions.question_text: Changing the reference height in the sim affects:
options: The value of gravitational potential energy measured
questions.correct_answer: The value of gravitational potential energy measured
questions.explanation: Reference level defines zero PE; changing it shifts PE values.

questions.question_text: At the lowest point of the track (no friction), the skater's speed is:
questions.explanation: Maximum KE (and speed) occurs where PE is minimum.

questions.question_text: The law of conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed.
questions.explanation: Total energy in an isolated system is conserved.

questions.question_text: Adding friction causes the total mechanical energy of the skater to:
questions.explanation: Some mechanical energy is lost as thermal energy due to friction.

questions.question_text: Name two forms of energy displayed in the energy bar chart.
questions.explanation: The sim shows kinetic, gravitational potential, and thermal energy.

questions.question_text: As height increases, what happens to gravitational potential energy?
questions.explanation: Gravitational PE increases with height: PE = mgh.

question_bank.title: Balloons and Static Electricity — Physics Assessment

questions.question_text: Rubbing the balloon on the sweater transfers charge mainly by:
questions.explanation: Rubbing transfers electrons between materials by friction.

questions.question_text: Two balloons with the same type of charge will:
questions.explanation: Like charges repel each other.

questions.question_text: Objects with opposite types of charge will:
questions.explanation: Unlike charges attract each other.

questions.question_text: An insulator does not allow charge to move easily through it.
questions.explanation: In insulators, electrons are not free to move throughout the material.

questions.question_text: A charged balloon is brought near a neutral wall and sticks because of:
options: Induced charge separation in the wall
questions.correct_answer: Induced charge separation in the wall
questions.explanation: The charged balloon induces opposite charge near the surface, causing attraction.

questions.question_text: When the balloon is rubbed on the sweater, electrons are transferred between the two objects.
questions.explanation: Charging by friction involves electron transfer.

questions.question_text: In the simulation, the balloon and sweater are examples of:
questions.explanation: Rubber and wool are insulating materials in this context.

questions.question_text: If both balloons have negative charge, they will:
questions.explanation: Like negative charges repel.

questions.question_text: What is meant by charging by friction?
questions.explanation: Charging by friction is the transfer of electrons when two materials are rubbed together.

questions.question_text: What happens when a charged balloon is brought near a neutral wall?
questions.explanation: Induced charges cause attraction between the balloon and the wall.

questions.question_text: Ohm's Law is written as:
questions.explanation: Voltage equals current multiplied by resistance.

questions.question_text: If voltage is kept constant and resistance is doubled, the current:
questions.explanation: From I = V/R, current is inversely proportional to resistance.

questions.question_text: The SI unit of electrical resistance is the:
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).

questions.question_text: The SI unit of electric current is the:
questions.explanation: Current is measured in amperes (A).

questions.question_text: For an ohmic conductor, voltage is directly proportional to current when resistance is constant.
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law: V ∝ I when R is fixed.

questions.question_text: Resistance measures how much a component opposes the flow of electric current.
questions.explanation: Higher resistance means less current for the same voltage.

questions.question_text: If resistance is constant and voltage is doubled, the current:
questions.explanation: Current is directly proportional to voltage when R is constant.

questions.question_text: On a voltage–current graph for an ohmic resistor, the slope represents:
questions.explanation: From V = IR, slope ΔV/ΔI equals R.

questions.question_text: State Ohm's Law as an equation.
questions.explanation: Voltage = current × resistance.

questions.question_text: Name two electrical quantities you can adjust in the Ohm's Law simulation.
questions.explanation: The sim allows adjustment of voltage and resistance to observe current.
